units.title: Preferences and Utility
units.blurb: How economists describe what people want: preference axioms, indifference curves, utility functions and the marginal rate of substitution.

units.title: Consumer Choice
units.blurb: Budget sets, the best affordable bundle, corners and kinks, the Lagrange method, minimizing spending, and revealed preference.

units.title: Demand and Welfare
units.blurb: How demand responds to income and prices, income and substitution effects, point elasticity, market demand, and money measures of gains and losses.

units.title: Work, Time and Risk
units.blurb: Choosing between work and leisure, between now and later, and among risky prospects.

units.title: Production and Cost
units.blurb: Production functions with calculus, isoquants, returns to scale, cost minimization and cost functions.

units.title: Competitive Markets
units.blurb: The firm's supply curve, producer surplus, long-run equilibrium with free entry, and the incidence and cost of taxes.

units.title: Market Power
units.blurb: Monopoly with calculus, markups and the Lerner index, pricing in separate markets, two-part tariffs and monopsony.

units.title: Game Theory and Strategy
units.blurb: Nash equilibrium in pure and mixed strategies, sequential and repeated games, oligopoly models and auctions.

units.title: General Equilibrium and Welfare
units.blurb: Trade between two people in an Edgeworth box, competitive equilibrium in exchange, and the two welfare theorems.

units.title: Externalities and Information
units.blurb: Externalities with calculus, the Coase theorem, public goods, common resources, adverse selection, moral hazard and signaling.

topics.title: Preferences and Their Axioms
topics.short: Completeness, transitivity, more-is-better and a taste for variety let us rank bundles of goods consistently.
topics.trouble: Students think rational preferences must be selfish or sensible. The axioms ask only that rankings be complete and consistent, whatever a person likes.

topics.title: Indifference Curves
topics.short: All bundles a person likes equally lie on one curve; when more is better, the curves slope down and never cross.
topics.trouble: Students draw indifference curves that cross, or read a higher curve as having more of every good rather than as being preferred.

topics.title: Utility Functions
topics.short: A utility function gives preferred bundles bigger numbers; any increasing transformation of it describes the same preferences.
topics.trouble: Students treat utility as measured happiness ("twice as happy"), when only the ranking of bundles matters.

topics.title: Marginal Utility as a Partial Derivative
topics.short: MUx = ∂U/∂x is the extra utility from a little more x with y held fixed.
topics.trouble: Students differentiate with respect to both goods at once, or set the other good to zero instead of holding it constant.

topics.title: The Marginal Rate of Substitution
topics.short: MRS = MUx/MUy, the amount of y a person would give up for one more x, is the size of the indifference curve's slope.
topics.trouble: Students write MUy/MUx, flipping the ratio, or forget that the MRS changes as you move along a curved indifference curve.

topics.title: Substitutes, Complements, Cobb-Douglas and Quasilinear
topics.short: Four common utility functions and the shapes of their indifference curves.
topics.trouble: Students expect every indifference curve to be smoothly bowed, and so apply the tangency rule to perfect substitutes or perfect complements, where it fails.

topics.title: Budget Sets
topics.short: p₁x₁ + p₂x₂ ≤ m, and how prices, income, taxes and rationing reshape the set of affordable bundles.
topics.trouble: Students shift the budget line in parallel when one price changes. A change in one price rotates the line around the intercept on the other good's axis.

topics.title: The Best Affordable Bundle
topics.short: At an interior optimum the MRS equals the price ratio; substitute the budget into the utility function and maximize.
topics.trouble: Students set the MRS equal to the price ratio upside down (p₂/p₁), or find a tangency point that is not on the budget line.

topics.title: Cobb-Douglas Demand
topics.short: With U = xᵃyᵇ a person spends the fixed share a/(a + b) of income on x.
topics.trouble: Students expect the quantity of x to depend on the price of y. With Cobb-Douglas utility it does not.

topics.title: Corners and Kinks
topics.short: Perfect substitutes lead to buying only the good with more utility per dollar; perfect complements are bought in fixed proportions.
topics.trouble: Students set the MRS equal to the price ratio for perfect substitutes and get no answer or a wrong mix, instead of comparing marginal utility per dollar.

topics.title: The Lagrange Method for Consumers
topics.short: Maximize utility subject to the budget with a Lagrange multiplier, which measures the marginal utility of income.
topics.trouble: Students solve the first-order conditions but forget the budget constraint, leaving more unknowns than equations.

topics.title: Minimizing Spending for a Target Utility
topics.short: The cheapest way to reach a utility level is also a tangency, and it gives compensated (Hicksian) demand.
topics.trouble: Students expect a different tangency rule for minimizing spending. The condition MRS = p₁/p₂ is the same; only the constraint changes.

topics.title: Revealed Preference
topics.short: If you chose bundle A when B was affordable, you should never choose B when A is affordable.
topics.trouble: Students check only whether the chosen bundles differ, not whether each one was affordable when the other was chosen.

topics.title: Income Changes and Engel Curves
topics.short: The income offer curve and the Engel curve show normal goods, inferior goods, luxuries and necessities.
topics.trouble: Students treat "inferior" as a fixed label, when a good can be normal at low incomes and inferior at high ones.

topics.title: Price Changes and the Demand Curve
topics.short: Rotating the budget line traces the price offer curve and the demand curve; doubling all prices and income changes nothing.
topics.trouble: Students treat every inferior good as a Giffen good. A Giffen good needs an income effect strong enough to outweigh the substitution effect.

topics.title: Substitution and Income Effects
topics.short: Split a price change into a move along the original indifference curve and a shift from the change in buying power.
topics.trouble: Students think the income effect always works in the same direction as the substitution effect. For an inferior good it works against it.

topics.title: Point Elasticity with Calculus
topics.short: ε = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) at a point; demand Q = AP^(−k) has elasticity −k everywhere.
topics.trouble: Students use the slope dQ/dP alone as the elasticity, or use dP/dQ when the demand curve is written with P in terms of Q.

topics.title: Adding Up to Market Demand
topics.short: Market demand adds the quantities all buyers want at each price, a horizontal sum.
topics.trouble: Students add the prices instead of the quantities, or miss the kink where a second buyer starts buying.

topics.title: Consumer Surplus as an Integral
topics.short: Consumer surplus is the area under the demand curve and above the price, an integral over quantity.
topics.trouble: Students integrate the demand curve from zero without subtracting the price, which gives total willingness to pay instead of surplus.

topics.title: Compensating and Equivalent Variation
topics.short: Money measures of a price change: how much to hand back afterward (CV) or take away beforehand (EV) to leave utility the same.
topics.trouble: Students assume CV, EV and the change in consumer surplus are always equal. They match only when there is no income effect, as with quasilinear utility.

topics.title: Labor Supply and Leisure
topics.short: A higher wage makes leisure more costly but also makes you richer, so labor supply can bend backward.
topics.trouble: Students assume a higher wage always means more hours worked, forgetting the income effect on leisure.

topics.title: Present Value
topics.short: A dollar later is worth less than a dollar now: PV = FV/(1 + r)ᵗ, with shortcuts for annuities and perpetuities.
topics.trouble: Students multiply by (1 + r)ᵗ when they should divide, or discount over the wrong number of periods.

topics.title: Saving and Borrowing over Time
topics.short: The budget c₁ + c₂/(1 + r) = m₁ + m₂/(1 + r) shows when it pays to save and when to borrow.
topics.trouble: Students think a higher interest rate must make every saver save more. For a saver, the income effect can push the other way.

topics.title: Expected Utility
topics.short: Compare risky choices by the probability-weighted average of their utilities, not of their dollar amounts.
topics.trouble: Students compute the utility of the expected value, U(E[W]), instead of the expected utility, E[U(W)].

topics.title: Risk Aversion and Certainty Equivalents
topics.short: With concave utility, a sure amount below the expected value is as good as the gamble; the gap is the risk premium.
topics.trouble: Students think a risk-averse person refuses every gamble. They accept gambles whose expected gain is large enough to cover the risk premium.

topics.title: Insurance
topics.short: A risk-averse person offered actuarially fair insurance buys full coverage.
topics.trouble: Students think insurance is a bad buy whenever the premium is above the expected loss, ignoring what removing the risk is worth to a risk-averse buyer.

topics.title: Production Functions and Marginal Products
topics.short: Q = f(K, L); the marginal product of labor is ∂Q/∂L.
topics.trouble: Students treat the marginal product as output per worker, which is the average product.

topics.title: Isoquants and the MRTS
topics.short: An isoquant shows the input mixes that make the same output; the size of its slope is MRTS = MPL/MPK.
topics.trouble: Students flip the ratio to MPK/MPL, or think an isoquant shows input mixes with equal cost.

topics.title: Returns to Scale
topics.short: Doubling every input may more than double, exactly double, or less than double output.
topics.trouble: Students confuse returns to scale (all inputs grow together) with diminishing marginal product (one input grows alone), and conclude that diminishing marginal products mean decreasing returns to scale.

topics.title: Cost Minimization
topics.short: The cheapest input mix sets MRTS = w/r, the producer's version of the consumer's tangency.
topics.trouble: Students set the MRTS equal to r/w, or put all spending on whichever input is cheaper per unit.

topics.title: Cost Functions and Marginal Cost
topics.short: C(q) gives the least cost of making q; MC = C′(q) and AC = C(q)/q.
topics.trouble: Students differentiate average cost to get marginal cost, or let fixed cost show up in marginal cost.

topics.title: Short-Run and Long-Run Cost
topics.short: With capital fixed, short-run cost is never below long-run cost; the long-run curve is the lower envelope of the short-run curves.
topics.trouble: Students think the long-run average cost curve passes through the lowest point of every short-run curve. It touches each one only at the output where that plant size is best.

topics.title: Where Average Cost Is Lowest
topics.short: Average cost is lowest where it equals marginal cost, and the quotient rule shows why.
topics.trouble: Students set marginal cost to zero to find the lowest average cost.

topics.title: The Competitive Firm's Supply Curve
topics.short: Maximize pq − C(q): set p = MC on the rising part of MC above minimum average variable cost.
topics.trouble: Students take the whole MC curve as the supply curve, including its falling part and the part below minimum AVC.

topics.title: Producer Surplus as an Integral
topics.short: Producer surplus is the integral of p − MC, which equals revenue minus variable cost, or profit plus fixed cost.
topics.trouble: Students equate producer surplus with profit, forgetting that fixed cost comes out of profit but not out of producer surplus.

topics.title: Long-Run Industry Equilibrium
topics.short: With free entry, price falls to minimum average cost, and the number of firms is market quantity over each firm's output.
topics.trouble: Students let the price stay above minimum average cost in the long run, or count firms using the short-run output per firm.

topics.title: Tax Incidence with Elasticities
topics.short: Buyers bear the share εS/(εS + |εD|) of a small per-unit tax, so the less elastic side pays more.
topics.trouble: Students give the larger share of the tax to the more elastic side, turning the formula upside down.

topics.title: Deadweight Loss of a Tax
topics.short: The deadweight loss is about ½·t·ΔQ, so it grows with the square of the tax.
topics.trouble: Students expect doubling a tax to double its deadweight loss. With straight-line curves it quadruples.

topics.title: Monopoly with Calculus
topics.short: Maximize p(q)·q − C(q): set MR = p + q·p′(q) equal to MC.
topics.trouble: Students set price equal to marginal cost, or differentiate p(q)·q as p′(q) alone, forgetting the product rule.

topics.title: Markups and the Lerner Index
topics.short: (p − MC)/p = 1/|ε|, so a monopoly with positive marginal cost never prices where demand is inelastic.
topics.trouble: Students think a firm with market power picks a price where demand is inelastic. When marginal cost is positive, demand is always elastic at the profit-maximizing price.

topics.title: Pricing in Separate Markets
topics.short: Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost in each market; the less elastic market pays the higher price.
topics.trouble: Students set the prices, rather than the marginal revenues, equal across markets, or charge more in the more elastic market.

topics.title: Two-Part Tariffs
topics.short: With identical customers, charge a per-unit price equal to marginal cost and an entry fee equal to each customer's consumer surplus.
topics.trouble: Students keep the monopoly per-unit price and add a fee, which earns less than pricing at marginal cost and capturing the larger surplus with the fee.

topics.title: Monopsony with Calculus
topics.short: An employer facing the wage curve w(L) hires where marginal revenue product equals the marginal cost of labor, w + L·w′(L).
topics.trouble: Students read the wage from the marginal cost of labor at the chosen L instead of from the supply curve w(L).

topics.title: Best Responses and Nash Equilibrium
topics.short: Mark each player's best responses; any cell where both are best responses is a Nash equilibrium, and there may be several.
topics.trouble: Students stop after finding one equilibrium, missing that coordination games have two or more.

topics.title: Mixed Strategies
topics.short: In a mixed-strategy equilibrium each player mixes so as to make the other player indifferent between their choices.
topics.trouble: Students find a player's mixing probabilities from that player's own payoffs. They come from the other player's payoffs.

topics.title: Sequential Games and Backward Induction
topics.short: Solve a game tree from the end: each player looks ahead to how others will respond, which rules out empty threats.
topics.trouble: Students solve the tree from the top down, or believe a threat that would hurt the player who carries it out.

topics.title: Repeated Games and Cooperation
topics.short: When a game repeats with no known last round, cooperation can last if players value the future enough.
topics.trouble: Students think a big payoff from cooperating is enough. Cooperation lasts only if the discount factor is high enough that the future loss from punishment outweighs the one-time gain from cheating.

topics.title: Cournot Competition
topics.short: Firms choose quantities; each firm's best response depends on the other's output, and equilibrium output lies between monopoly and competition.
topics.trouble: Students maximize each firm's profit as if it were a monopoly, leaving the rival's output out of the price.

topics.title: Bertrand Competition
topics.short: Two firms selling identical goods and competing on price drive the price down to marginal cost.
topics.trouble: Students expect two firms to keep prices well above cost, as in Cournot. With identical goods and price competition, undercutting continues until P = MC.

topics.title: Stackelberg Leadership
topics.short: A leader who moves first, knowing the follower's best response, produces more and earns more than in Cournot.
topics.trouble: Students give the leader its Cournot best response, forgetting that the leader plugs in the follower's reaction before maximizing.

topics.title: Auctions
topics.short: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy; in a first-price auction bidders shade their bids.
topics.trouble: Students shade their bids in a second-price auction, which can only cost them a profitable win.

topics.title: The Edgeworth Box and Pareto Efficiency
topics.short: An allocation is Pareto efficient when no trade can help one person without hurting the other; there the two MRSs are equal.
topics.trouble: Students think Pareto efficient means fair. An allocation that gives everything to one person is Pareto efficient.

topics.title: Competitive Equilibrium in Exchange
topics.short: Find the price ratio at which both people's demands, paid for with the value of their endowments, add up to what is available.
topics.trouble: Students treat income as a fixed number of dollars, forgetting that each person's income is the value of their endowment at the very prices being solved for.

topics.title: The Welfare Theorems
topics.short: Competitive equilibria are Pareto efficient, and with convex preferences any efficient allocation can be reached with lump-sum transfers.
topics.trouble: Students read the first welfare theorem as saying markets give fair results, or forget its conditions: no externalities, no market power and full information.

topics.title: The Efficient Amount of an Externality
topics.short: Set marginal benefit equal to marginal social cost; a tax equal to the marginal external damage at that quantity gets the market there.
topics.trouble: Students set the tax equal to the marginal damage at the market quantity rather than at the efficient quantity.

topics.title: The Coase Theorem
topics.short: With clear property rights and low bargaining costs, the parties reach the efficient outcome whoever holds the rights; only who pays whom differs.
topics.trouble: Students think the efficient amount of the harmful activity depends on who holds the right, when (with no income effects) the right decides only who pays whom.

topics.title: Providing Public Goods Efficiently
topics.short: Provide more of a public good while the sum of everyone's marginal benefits is above its marginal cost.
topics.trouble: Students add demand curves horizontally, as for private goods, instead of vertically, even though everyone uses the same units of a public good.

topics.title: Common Resources
topics.short: Open access draws users until the average return equals the cost, which uses the resource more than is efficient.
topics.trouble: Students expect open access to give the efficient level of use because each user is rational. Each one ignores the cost their use imposes on the others.

topics.title: Adverse Selection and Lemons
topics.short: When sellers know quality and buyers don't, good products can be driven out of the market.
topics.trouble: Students mix up adverse selection (hidden information before a deal) with moral hazard (hidden actions after it).

topics.title: Moral Hazard and Incentives
topics.short: When actions are hidden after a deal, deductibles, copays and pay tied to results can restore incentives.
topics.trouble: Students call any risky behavior moral hazard, rather than behavior that changes because someone else now bears the cost.

topics.title: Signaling
topics.short: A costly signal can separate types when it costs the high type less, even if it adds nothing to productivity.
topics.trouble: Students think a signal works only if it raises productivity. It works when it costs the low type more than imitating the high type is worth.
